patient.chief_complaint: Found confused and unresponsive in nursing home, brief shaking 2 hours ago, now 'awake' but disoriented
patient.hpi: A 71-year-old African American male was transferred from a skilled nursing facility to the emergency department after nursing staff found him minimally responsive in his bed during morning rounds. A nursing aide reported witnessing him shake briefly — 'his whole body was stiff and then rhythmically jerking' — for about 90 seconds approximately 2 hours before presentation. He was incontinent of urine during the episode. After the shaking stopped, he did not return to his baseline. He is a nursing home resident with moderate vascular dementia, prior stroke, and multiple medical comorbidities. At baseline per staff, he speaks in short sentences, recognizes his daughter, and follows simple commands. On arrival to the ED he is awake with eyes open but stares blankly, does not respond to his name, and produces only incomprehensible sounds. Nursing home staff reports he has had no fever or vomiting. Medications were administered per chart: none missed. His carbamazepine was recently increased 3 weeks ago from 200 mg BID to 400 mg BID by his neurologist for worsening behavioral symptoms attributed to frontal lobe seizures. Family reports he had a known large left MCA territory ischemic stroke 4 years ago, leaving him with right hemiparesis and aphasia. He also has atrial fibrillation managed with apixaban. He is on carbamazepine for post-stroke epilepsy. His daughter is present and states his confusion seems different from his usual post-seizure state — 'He usually comes back within 20 minutes. It's been hours now.'

past_medical_history: Left MCA territory ischemic stroke 4 years ago — chronic right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia

medications.frequency: twice daily (recently increased from 200 mg BID 3 weeks ago)

social_history.note: Retired postal worker. Widower. Resides in skilled nursing facility for 2 years since stroke left him unable to care for himself. Non-smoker, no alcohol, no illicit drugs.

eeg.impression: ABNORMAL EEG. NCSE arising from left temporal-parietal region on background of chronic left hemisphere encephalomalacia. Electrographic seizures with LPDs meeting NCSE criteria. Superimposed GPDs with triphasic morphology may indicate metabolic contribution. Urgent IV benzodiazepine trial advised. Clinical correlation recommended.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: WBC 12.4 x10^9/L (H), Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (L), Sodium 132 mEq/L (L), Chloride 96 mEq/L (L), CO2 20 mEq/L (L), BUN 28 mg/dL (H), Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (H), Glucose 142 mg/dL (H), Carbamazepine 14.2 mcg/mL (H), Urine sodium 62 mEq/L (H), Urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg (L), Lactate 3.6 mmol/L (H), CK 580 U/L (H).

findings.location: left MCA territory — frontal, temporal, parietal cortex

ct.impression: Chronic left MCA territory encephalomalacia from prior stroke. No acute intracranial hemorrhage. No new structural lesion. CT does not explain worsening encephalopathy — EEG-confirmed NCSE and metabolic derangement (hyponatremia) are primary.
recommended_actions: MRI not immediately required given known chronic changes on CT and established NCSE diagnosis via EEG
Correct hyponatremia cautiously — goal increase 0.5-1 mEq/L per hour, maximum 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination

output.impression: NCSE resolved with combined treatment: hyponatremia correction + lacosamide loading. Residual LPDs on chronic left hemisphere background. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions.description: Carbamazepine is a well-established cause of SIADH via ADH-sensitizing effect on renal tubules. Risk increases with higher doses. The recent dose increase from 200 to 400 mg BID dramatically increased SIADH risk. Sertraline (SSRI) also causes SIADH — dual SIADH mechanism increases sodium-lowering risk.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Discontinue carbamazepine as AED of choice. Switch to lacosamide (no SIADH). Monitor sodium closely if oxcarbazepine considered (higher SIADH risk than CBZ). If SSRI needed, consider non-SIADH-risk agent or monitor sodium monthly.

output.summary: Dual SIADH mechanism: carbamazepine dose increase + sertraline both cause SIADH. The combination precipitated Na 132, lowering seizure threshold and causing NCSE despite supratherapeutic CBZ levels. AED switch to lacosamide recommended.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure: 18 cmH2O. WBC: 4 cells/mm3 (lymphocytes) (N/A PMN/N/A lymph). Protein: 48 mg/dL (mildly elevated). Glucose: 76 mg/dL (ratio 0.54). Anti-NMDAR IgG: Negative. Anti-LGI1 IgG: Negative. HSV PCR: Negative. Gram stain: No organisms. Culture: No growth.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) secondary to carbamazepine-induced SIADH causing hyponatremia (Na 132), precipitating breakthrough seizures from chronic post-stroke epileptogenic focus

differential.key_features: Duration >2 hours without return to baseline; EEG confirms ongoing NCSE, not simple post-ictal state
Sodium 132 can cause confusion; however EEG shows clear electrographic seizure activity (NCSE not just encephalopathy); both diagnoses coexist — SIADH caused NCSE
CT shows no new changes; known chronic left MCA encephalomalacia; no acute DWI restriction
Autoimmune panel negative; clear etiology (post-stroke epilepsy + CBZ-SIADH hyponatremia); no lymphocytic pleocytosis or temporal MRI changes

optimal_actions.action: Emergent EEG to distinguish NCSE from prolonged post-ictal state or metabolic encephalopathy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left temporal NCSE with LPDs on chronic encephalomalacia background

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head to exclude hemorrhage (urgent given anticoagulated patient on apixaban)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Chronic left MCA encephalomalacia; no new hemorrhage

optimal_actions.action: Obtain labs including BMP (sodium critical), CBC, AED levels (carbamazepine), urine sodium + osmolality to evaluate SIADH
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Na 132; carbamazepine supratherapeutic; SIADH pattern (urine Na >40, urine Osm >100)

optimal_actions.action: Administer IV lorazepam 2 mg for NCSE; note partial response on EEG (CBZ-SIADH hyponatremia must also be corrected)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Partial NCSE suppression — hyponatremia must also be corrected

optimal_actions.action: Initiate hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) or isotonic saline fluid restriction for SIADH-related hyponatremia — correct Na at 0.5-1 mEq/L/hr, maximum 8-10 mEq/24h
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sodium correction to 136-138 mEq/L over 24-48 hours

optimal_actions.action: Load IV lacosamide 400 mg as second-line AED — preferred over phenytoin (no SIADH, no cardiac risk in elderly with AF)
Check drug interactions — identify carbamazepine + sertraline dual SIADH mechanism
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Dual SIADH risk: carbamazepine + sertraline — switch CBZ to lacosamide

optimal_actions.action: Switch carbamazepine to lacosamide for chronic epilepsy management — eliminate SIADH risk
Continuous cEEG monitoring 24-48 hours to confirm NCSE resolution
optimal_actions.expected_finding: NCSE resolved after sodium correction + lacosamide

critical_actions: Emergent EEG — NCSE diagnosis requires EEG in confused post-stroke patient
Check serum sodium and carbamazepine level immediately — CBZ-SIADH is the primary precipitant
Correct hyponatremia carefully — max 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination
Switch carbamazepine to lacosamide to eliminate ongoing SIADH risk
IV lorazepam + IV lacosamide for NCSE — benzodiazepine alone insufficient
contraindicated_actions: Increasing carbamazepine dose — supratherapeutic CBZ is causing SIADH; increasing would worsen hyponatremia
Rapid sodium correction (>10-12 mEq/24h) — risk osmotic demyelination syndrome, especially in elderly
Using phenytoin as second-line AED — risk of cardiac arrhythmia in elderly AF patient; also no benefit for CBZ-SIADH-related NCSE
Fluid restriction alone without AED — NCSE requires both metabolic correction and AED treatment
key_reasoning_points: Carbamazepine-induced SIADH is a class effect of all sodium channel-affecting AEDs (CBZ, OXC); dose increase from 200 to 400 mg BID tripled SIADH risk
Sertraline (SSRI) dual SIADH mechanism compounds the hyponatremia risk — combination caused sodium to drop to 132
NCSE diagnostic pearl: EEG essential in any confused post-stroke patient with known epilepsy — 'prolonged post-ictal' should never be assumed without EEG
CBZ-SIADH paradox: supratherapeutic CBZ level (14.2 mcg/mL) despite NCSE — the drug causing SIADH hyponatremia is also not controlling seizures adequately
Lacosamide is the preferred AED switch: no SIADH risk, safe in AF (no cardiac toxicity), therapeutic at moderate doses in CKD stage 3
Sodium correction rate is critical — elderly with chronic hyponatremia require slow correction to prevent osmotic demyelination

metadata.teaching_points: Carbamazepine-SIADH hyponatremia causing NCSE; dual SIADH with SSRI; AED switch to lacosamide; sodium correction rate in elderly
metadata.pitfalls: Increasing CBZ dose when SIADH hyponatremia is the cause; rapid sodium correction; attributing confusion to post-ictal or dementia without EEG
metadata.clinical_pearl: Carbamazepine + SSRI = dual SIADH mechanism. Supratherapeutic CBZ causing hyponatremia = paradoxical NCSE. Switch to lacosamide eliminates SIADH risk.
